q-163682.name: Question 1
q-163682.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(2-x)\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
q-163682.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2(2)-\frac{1}{2}({2}^{2})-(2(1)-\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2})) \\  & =4-2-2+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis under the action of a force of magnitude (2−x)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=1 to x=2.

a
1J
b
32J
c
3J
d
2J
e
12J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work done by a force F=F(x) in moving a particle from x=x1 to x=x2 is given by W=∫x1x2F(x)dx.

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules (J).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain W=∫12(2−x)dx=[2x−12x2]12=2(2)−12(22)−(2(1)−12(12))=4−2−2+12=12J.

q-163686.name: Question 2
q-163686.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(3\sqrt{x}+2)\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=4.$
q-163686.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3\sqrt{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{1/2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3/2}+2x]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2({4}^{3/2})+2(4)-(2({1}^{3/2})+2(1)) \\  & =16+8-2-2 \\  & =20\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163688.name: Question 3
q-163688.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $0.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(5-x)\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
q-163688.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $0.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(5-x)\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=0.5\cdot (5-x)=(2.5-0.5x)\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(2.5-0.5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{5}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(2)-\frac{1}{4}({2}^{2})-(\frac{5}{2}(1)-\frac{1}{4}({1}^{2})) \\  & =5-1-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163597.name: Question 4
q-163597.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $1.5\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis with an acceleration of magnitude $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}$ acting in the direction $OP.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
q-163597.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $1.5\,kg$ at a rate of $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}$ is

$$
F=ma=1.5\cdot (2x+1)=(3x+1.5)\,N.
$$

Now, substituting the known values into our integral, we obtain

$$

q-163687.name: Question 5
q-163687.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-{x}^{3})\,\text{N}$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=2.$
q-163687.worked_solution:
The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[8x-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =8(2)-\frac{1}{4}({2}^{4})-(8(1)-\frac{1}{4}({1}^{4})) \\  & =16-4-8+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{17}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163598.name: Question 6
q-163598.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $2t\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
q-163598.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int 2t\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & ={t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0={0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)={2}^{2}=4\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {4}^{2} \\  & =16\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P of mass 3kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude 3tm/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time t=1s.

a
12J
b
9J
c
6J
d
3J
e
15J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The kinetic energy of a particle with mass m and velocity v is given by KE=12mv2.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫3tdtv(t)=2t3/2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 0=2(03/2)+C⟹C=0.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=2t3/2. In particular, its velocity at time t=1s is v=v(1)=2(13/2)=2m/s.

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at t=1 is KE=12mv2=12⋅3⋅22=6J.

q-163713.name: Question 8
q-163713.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{t+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the particle between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$
q-163713.worked_solution:
The change in kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m,$ initial velocity ${v}_{0},$ and final velocity ${v}_{1}$ is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|t+1|.$ In particular, its inital velocity at time $t=1\,s$ and final velocity at time $t=3\,s$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+1|=\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s, \\ {v}_{1} & =v(3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|3+1|=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the particle between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ\,\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2} \\  & =8{ln}^{2}⁡2-2{ln}^{2}⁡2 \\  & =6{ln}^{2}⁡(2)\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163704.name: Question 9
q-163704.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $8\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=3\,s.$
q-163704.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-\frac{1}{t+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-\frac{1}{0+1}+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1-\frac{1}{t+1}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=3\,s$ is

$$
v=v(3)=1-\frac{1}{3+1}=\frac{3}{4}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {(\frac{3}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot \frac{9}{16} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

A particle P of mass 8kg moves along the x-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude 1(t+1)2m/s2, where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing x, and t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time t=3s.

a
32J
b
94J
c
6J
d
2J
e
4J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The kinetic energy of a particle with mass m and velocity v is given by KE=12mv2.

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules (J).

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dtv(t)=∫1(t+1)2dtv(t)=−1t+1+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 0=−10+1+C⟹C=1.

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time t is v(t)=1−1t+1. In particular, its velocity at time t=3s is v=v(3)=1−13+1=34m/s.

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at t=3 is KE=12mv2=12⋅8⋅(34)2=12⋅8⋅916=94J.

q-163709.name: Question 10
q-163709.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $\frac{3}{2}\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $(1+2t)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=2\,s.$
q-163709.worked_solution:
The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int (1+2t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =t+{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=0+{0}^{2}+C\,⟹\,C=0.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=t+{t}^{2}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=2\,s$ is

$$
v=v(2)=2+{2}^{2}=6\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot 36 \\  & =27\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163663.name: Question 11
q-163663.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $3\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $({t}^{2}+t+1)\,m,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=0\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
q-163663.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)={t}^{2}+t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+1) \\  & =2t+1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=0$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(0)=2(0)+1=1\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)+1=5\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{75}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =36\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

q-163674.name: Question 12
q-163674.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by $({t}^{3}+2)\,m,$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=2\,s$ and $t=3\,s.$
q-163674.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by $x(t)={t}^{3}+2,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+2) \\  & =3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(2)=3(2)^{2}=12\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=3$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(3)=3(3)^{2}=27\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$

A particle P of mass 2kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The displacement of the particle is given by (t3+2)m, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times t=2s and t=3s.

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The displacement of the particle is given by x(t)=t3+2, where t is time in seconds. We find the velocity v(t) of the particle by differentiating the displacement with respect to time:

v(t)=dxdt=ddt(t3+2)=3t2

So, the particle's initial velocity, at t=2, is v0=v(2)=3(2)2=12m/s, and final velocity, at t=3, is v1=v(3)=3(3)2=27m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅2⋅(27)2−12⋅2⋅(12)2=729−144=585J.

q-163671.html:
Question 15
?

A particle P of mass 1kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's velocity is (t+1)m/s, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. Calculate the work done by the force between the times t=2s and t=4s.

a
25J
b
17J
c
9J
d
8J
e
16J
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

The particle's velocity is given by v(t)=t+1, where t is time in seconds. So, the particle's initial velocity, at t=2, is v0=v(2)=2+1=3m/s, and final velocity, at t=4, is v1=v(4)=4+1=5m/s.

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

W=ΔKE=12⋅1⋅(5)2−12⋅1⋅(3)2=252−92=8J.

q-163666.name: Question 16
q-163666.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of the force of magnitude $(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that distances along the $x$-axis are measured in meters, the particle is initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=2,$ find the particle's change in velocity in moving from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
q-163666.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =16+16-0 \\  & =32\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=5\,m/s$ at $x=2.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {5}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 32 & =50-2{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2{v}_{0}^{2} & =18 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =9 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $3\,m/s.$

Finally, the particle's change in velocity from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is

$$
{v}_{1}-{v}_{0}=5-3=2\,m/s.
$$

q-163691.name: Question 17
q-163691.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $3{x}^{2}\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at $x=0,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=2.$
q-163691.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=0$ to $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{3}-0 \\  & =8\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at $x=0.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=2$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 8 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 8 & =2{v}_{1}^{2}-8 \\ 2{v}_{1}^{2} & =16 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =8 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=2$ is $2\sqrt{2}\,m/s.$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}+x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+1-0 \\  & =2\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{0}$ at $x=0$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}{m}_{1}{v}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {4}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 2 & =8-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =6 \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =12 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=0$ is $2\sqrt{3}\,m/s.$

Question 20
?

A particle P of mass 1kg moves along the x-axis under the action of the force of magnitude (3x2+1)N acting in the direction of increasing x. Given that x is measured in meters, the particle was initially at the origin, and the particle has velocity v=4m/s at x=1, calculate the particle's initial velocity.

a
3m/s
b
4m/s
c
22m/s
d
23m/s
e
32m/s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

W=ΔKE

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

ΔKE=12mv12−12mv02

and m is the particle's mass, v0 is its initial velocity, and v1 is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from x=0 to x=1:

W=∫x1x2F(x)dx=∫01(3x2+1)dx=x3+x|01=1+1−0=2J

The particle has velocity v=4m/s at x=1. So, we can find the velocity v0 at x=0 using the work-energy principle:

W=12m1v2−12mv022=12⋅1⋅42−12⋅1⋅v022=8−12v0212v02=6v02=12v0=±23.

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration.

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at x=0 is 23m/s.
